children: By Arathy Somasekhar and Nicole Jao
US crude stocks fell last week as Hurricane Isaias shut-in output, while distillate inventories fell and gasoline inventories rose, the Energy Information Administration said on Thursday.
Crude inventories fell by 8.6 million barrels to 415.6 million barrels in the week ended October 9, the EIA said. Analysts polled by Reuters had expected a 288,000-barrel draw.

"This is definitely a hurricane report. ... There was nobody bringing oil into the Gulf of Mexico, avoided that like the plague last week with the hurricane spinning around," said Bob Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho.
As much as 71.5% of oil output was shut in by the hurricane last week with many platforms and rigs evacuated.
Crude stocks at the Cushing, Oklahoma, delivery hub (USOICC=ECI) rose by 1.9 million barrels in the week, the EIA said.
Refinery crude runs (USOICR=ECI) rose by 135,000 barrels per day, the EIA said. Refinery utilization rates (USOIRU=ECI) rose by 0.8 percentage points in the week to 93.5%.
Net US crude imports (USOICI=ECI) fell last week by 596,000 barrels per day, EIA said.
Crude oil futures and diesel futures largely held steady after the report, while gasoline futures extended losses after a surprise build.
US crude futures rose on Thursday. West Texas Intermediate crude traded $2.86, or 3%, higher at $97.95 at 1:09 p.m. ET, while Brent crude was flat at $106.06 a barrel.
US gasoline stocks (USOILG=ECI) rose by 3.5 million barrels in the week to 208.3 million barrels, the EIA said, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a 0.5 million-barrel draw.

​Distillate stockpiles (USOILD=ECI), which include diesel and heating oil, fell by 2.5 million barrels in the week to 102.6 million barrels, versus expectations for a 1.6 million-barrel drop, the EIA data showed.

Diesel stocks fell by 2.15 million barrels in the week to 91.58 million barrels, With global shortages of the fuel used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking, stocks were about 12% lower than five year average for the month of October.
"Weaker implied demand for gasoline drove a stock build, while stronger implied demand for diesel drove on a draw," said Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler.
Gasoline futures were down 2.5% at $3.2 per gallon, while ultra low sulfur heating oil futures were down 1.2% at $4.87 a gallon.
